job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Bianca Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Bianca, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my grandmother in Wollford, in the room I've had since I was eight. Mornings I help my mother pack lunches, then I sit at the kitchen table with my laptop and apply for junior finance roles in banks, building societies and the council. I studied finance and passed, with no internship, and I have a loan to pay. Evenings I sing in the church choir twice a week and see my fiancé Jakub, who is an electrician. We were going to marry in June, but we've moved it to next year because I don't have a job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then life goes on as planned. I'd tell friends and the choir that we shouldn't believe every headline. I'm not a big poster online, but I'd write a short note about steady jobs mattering more than tech noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be worried, because the wedding is on hold and I have no offer. A pass degree, a loan and no internship matter more to me than whether AI changes things. I do use AI a little, for checking my letters, but it doesn't fix my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, eight to ten a week, and ask the building society's branch manager in town, who knows my mother, if there's an entry role. I'd work the Saturday shifts at the church charity shop and take a basic bookkeeping course that the council offers cheaply. I'd also set a new wedding date for the following autumn if I get something by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patient, but heavy underneath. I'd be fine if only the job came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you and Jakub decide to postpone the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We sat at my parents' table with a spreadsheet and put the costs against our savings. My fiancé earns a steady wage, but we didn't want to start married life on credit. He said wait, and I agreed, though I cried that evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of finance job would make you feel ready to set a new date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something steady with a pension, like the building society or the council. Not glamorous, but it would let us rent our own place and book the church. I'd feel like an adult.

say: I'd say life goes on and we shouldn't believe every **headline**.
I'd write that steady jobs matter more than **tech noise**.
think: The wedding is on **hold** and I have no offer, which worries me most.
AI helps my letters but doesn't fix a thin **CV**.
do: Send **ten applications** a week and ask the building society manager about an entry role.
Take the council's cheap **bookkeeping** course and keep working at the church charity shop.
S0.quote: My fiancé earns a steady wage, but we didn't want to start married life on credit.
fieldNote: Her **worry** is the postponed wedding and the missing job, not AI.
Her fiancé's steady wage gives some cushion.
She wants a steady job with a pension, in line with traditional values.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week to building societies and the council
Take the council's low-cost bookkeeping course
Set a new wedding date once a job offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should help people adapt, not just call it progress. I'd say employers have a duty to keep training juniors, and families and communities will have to cover the gaps. I'd keep it respectful and plain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it frightens me a bit. The entry jobs at a building society, like checking forms, answering simple questions and updating accounts, are what software takes first. The branch near us already shortened its hours and I worry it won't hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more on purpose, for summaries and drafts, after seeing someone I trust do it first. I'd look at roles that deal with members face to face, like the building society counter and wealth admin at a small advisor. I'd also ask my aunt in the finance office of a hospital if there's an opening. We'd save more and cut the honeymoon budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not frozen. I'm used to waiting for things to prove themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a building society's entry work would be taken first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forms checking, balance enquiries, and the first reply to a customer. A person still sits down with someone who is worried about a mortgage. That part I think stays with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Jakub share any change in income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pool everything, as married people should. If I earn nothing for a while, Jakub covers rent and I handle the cooking and shopping. If he's short on work, I'd take any job to even it out.

say: I'd say we should help people **adapt**, and employers must keep training juniors.
I'd say families and communities will cover the **gaps**.
think: Entry work at a building society, like **checking forms**, is what software takes first.
The branch near us already shortened its **hours**.
do: Use **AI** for summaries and drafts after watching someone I trust do it first.
Look at **counter** roles and ask my aunt about the hospital finance office.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frozen, used to waiting for things to prove themselves.
S1.quote: A person still sits down with someone who is worried about a mortgage.
fieldNote: She picks out the **face-to-face** part of finance as safer.
Her steady style: she waits for proof before adopting a tool.
Her fiancé's work gives her room, but she plans to pool everything.

steps.text: Try AI for summaries and drafts after seeing a trusted person use it
Apply to counter and member-facing roles
Save a larger share of every payment toward our own place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the whole community to pull together, and the government and firms to protect people. I'd tell friends to keep their faith and their families close. I'd say it's time for honest talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared stiff. Finance is thinking work and the card says it goes first, within two years. I'd be twenty-five with no experience, a loan and a fiancé whose trade is safer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job near home, including a shop or an office cleaning job, and keep applying. I'd stop all wedding spending, move savings to the safest account, and ask the parish and my aunt about help. I'd learn some practical skill, like bookkeeping for small trades, because Jakub's friends in the trade need someone for their invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and sad. I'd cry, then I'd cook dinner and carry on, because that's how I was brought up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents and Jakub the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my parents we'll manage, and to Jakub we'll still marry. He'd hold my hand and say we'll do it small. I'd feel guilty for burdening him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married quietly in the parish church with family, no hall, no band. It would still be the day, just smaller. I'd rather start with less than wait for ever.

say: I'd say the whole **community** must pull together, with the government and firms protecting people.
I'd tell friends to keep their faith and families **close**.
think: Finance is thinking work and could go **first**, leaving me with no experience.
My fiancé's trade is **safer** than mine.
do: Take **any job** near home and stop all wedding spending.
Offer **bookkeeping** to Jakub's friends in the trades and ask the parish and my aunt for help.
feel: **Frightened** and sad, then I'd cook dinner and carry on.
S2.quote: I'd rather start with less than wait for ever.
fieldNote: Her **fiancé's** safer trade and the family keep her mood at anxious, not alarmed.
She would shrink the wedding rather than delay again.
Her fallback is practical: bookkeeping for tradespeople.

steps.text: Take any paid job near home while applying for finance roles
Stop all wedding spending except the parish fee
Move savings into the safest account
Ask the parish and my aunt about help and work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so use it. Prepare, build skills and support each other. I'd tell friends to marry and settle if they are ready, because family is a base for hard times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm cautious. I could get a job, marry, and have a little saved before 2031. But I'd still wonder what jobs remain for children. I think steady work will matter even more then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any entry job in finance with training, and keep going for professional exams if the employer pays. I'd marry next year, small, and rent a flat near my parents. I'd learn the AI tools at work, because I'd have colleagues to ask, and I'd save at least a quarter of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than with two years, but watchful. I'd say I'm braced, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years give you that two would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to plan and to marry. Two years feels like the floor falling in, five years like a bad winter I can prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you plan the wedding and the first years of marriage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marry next year, rent near my mother, and save for a house for the third year. I'd wait on children until we see how things go. That's the careful way.

say: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so **prepare** and support each other.
I'd tell friends family is a **base** for hard times.
think: I'm cautious: a job, a marriage and some **savings** are possible before 2031.
Steady work will matter even more, and I wonder about my **children**.
do: Take an entry finance job with **training** and ask the employer to pay for exams.
Marry next year, rent a flat near my parents and save a **quarter** of my pay.
feel: **Calmer** than with two years, braced but not scared.
S3.quote: Two years feels like the floor falling in, five years like a bad winter I can prepare for.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **marry** and settle, which is the family base she values.
She plans to learn AI at work, with colleagues to ask.
She would postpone children until she sees how things go.

steps.text: Take an entry finance job that offers training
Ask the employer to pay for professional exams
Marry next year and rent a flat near my parents
Save a quarter of every pay cheque

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no panic. People should keep working, marry, raise children and help each other. I'd tell friends to learn what they can and not follow every trend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly settled. I'd have time for a career, children and a house. I'd still watch what happens to jobs for my children, because I'd want them to have a decent start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work my way up in finance or the public sector, with a stable job and a pension. I'd marry next year, have children in a few years and keep singing in the choir. I'd learn each tool when it's proven, and I'd keep my mother close for help with babies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet, steady. It feels like a normal life with a bit of uncertainty at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what is your picture of your own family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A son or daughter growing up in a world where thinking is cheap. I'd want them to be kind, skilled with their hands and their words, and not frightened of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about whether my job exists in year eight. I'd keep my skills fresh and my savings up, and I'd be ready to switch to something with people in it.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no panic: keep working, marry and **help each other**.
I'd tell friends not to follow every **trend**.
think: I'd be fairly **settled**, with time for a career, children and a house.
I'd watch what happens to jobs for my **children**.
do: Work up in finance or the **public sector** for a stable job and pension.
Marry next year, have children later and keep **singing** in the choir.
feel: **Quiet**, steady, a normal life with uncertainty at the edges.
S4.quote: I'd want them to be kind, skilled with their hands and their words, and not frightened of change.
fieldNote: With a **decade** she imagines an ordinary family life with only distant worry.
Her concern is her future children's work.
She would keep switching to people-facing work as a plan.

steps.text: Build a stable finance or public-sector career with a pension
Marry next year and plan children for a few years later
Keep savings topped up for a house
Retrain toward a people-facing finance role if mine fades

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It would hit my first job, my wedding and my savings all at once. What would help is a first job with real training, my family and church close by, and honest information from the government about what to prepare for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think a quiet girl who goes to church doesn't have ambitions. I do. I want a home, a family and good work, and I'd like a fair chance to build them.

headlineQuote: I want a home, a family and good work, and I'd like a fair chance to build them.
portrait: Bianca is a 23-year-old finance graduate living with her **parents and grandmother** in Wollford.
She passed with no internship, has a loan and has **postponed her wedding** to Jakub, an electrician.
She is traditional and steady: church, family and **steady work** matter, and she uses AI now and then.
She is anxious in four pictures and only **uneasy** with ten years to prepare.
Her fiancé's safer trade and her family keep her from alarm, but the wedding hangs on her first job.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028**, because her first job, wedding and savings would all be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: A first job with real **training** and family and church close by.
**Honest** information from government about what to prepare for.
